speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. SPEAKER  CORRECTION OF IMPRESSION CONVEYED BY RULING
speechtext:
I wonder if the house will allow me to make a correction in Hansard, not to the context but to the impression which I may have given inadvertently in dealing with a point of order at page 3662. The particular point of order was taken by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate when the Minister of Labour was seeking to refer to reports given by the unemployment insurance commission in 1955, and when defending himself with respect to allegations about his use of what was known as a supplementary report in the debate that was then proceeding.
After hearing some argument I find that altogether there were 24 separate interventions before I finally came to the point of giving my view, which I expressed in these terms:
The Prime Minister has expressed effectively the view which I had formed.
I was of course referring to the Prime Minister's immediately preceding intervention that it was in order for the minister to proceed to refer to the report, and not to matters in the other interventions which occurred earlier, four of which I find upon reading the report were also interventions by the Prime Minister. My endorsement was of his argument on the point of order in the intervention immediately preceding my own in the second column of page 3662.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED U.S. PROPOSAL FOR REDUCTION IN TEXTILE TARIFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the last session of congress legislation was enacted which empowered the United States administration to negotiate reductions in the United States tariffs of up to 20 per cent of existing rates over a four-year period in return for similar concessions on the part of other countries. The United States administration notified Canada and other GATT countries that they
[Mr. Herridge.l
would be prepared to enter on a first round of negotiations in the exercise of that power.
These negotiations cannot take place until the 1960 session of GATT, although it is contemplated at the 1959 session that there will be some preliminary discussions of a procedural nature looking forward to discussions in 1960 on United States proposals. subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour I have only a few more words to add to what I said last night when the committee adjourned. I was dealing at that time with unemployment fund questions and more general matters concerning employment. So far as the former are concerned, we on this side of the chamber will have an opportunity of asking questions in committee on this matter. We propose to take full advantage of that opportunity, particularly in regard to the management of investment funds, the evasion of the law in regard to reports and the status of the unemployment insurance advisory committee.
Not long ago I asked the Minister of Labour about the status of this committee, because I had previously made the statement that in my view it had no legal existence. The best I could get from the minister-and perhaps he will elaborate on the matter when he replies-was a reference to section 19, subsection 5 of the act, which states that a majority of members of the advisory committee constitute a quorum and a vacancy in the membership does not impair the right of the remaining members to act. With all due respect may I say that has nothing to do with the point I was making about the legal existence of the committee which is determined specifically in section 19, subsection 1, which say that the committee shall consist of a chairman and not less than six members, and there are not now six members of the committee.
I was also dealing last night with some questions arising out of a speech made by the Prime Minister on May 8 at Montreal which dealt with employment and labour matters among other things. It was a speech which was full of commercials and would have done credit to an advertising campaign.

Indeed, there is a very close connection between this speech and advertising, which makes it all the more unusual to hear the Prime Minister say in this speech that one of the faults of his party since it has been in office has been to take its good works too much for granted. If that is true, then the vice president in charge of advertising has not been doing his job.
On page 9 of this unusual speech the Prime Minister made a labour reference which perhaps should be put on the record. He said:
I can tell you that no group of men and women anywhere in Canada worked as hard or as many hours a day as the members of the cabinet.
The results of that work, according to the Prime Minister, were expressed in these words:
I have no hesitation in asserting at this time that I believe that the government has accomplished more in those two years than any other government at any time in our history.
He added:
The facts are on the record.
Indeed, that is true; the facts are on the record and the government can be judged by those facts put on the record in the last two years, facts which deal with unprecedented levels of unemployment since the thirties, unprecedented lack of confidence in government bonds and unprecedented tight money.
On page 15 of this speech the Prime Minister made mention of the unemployment insurance benefit question, to which I made a cursory reference previously. The Prime Minister referred to the dubious figure of $550 million in additional welfare funds that had been given to the Canadian people since this government came to office and said:
The $550 million does not include additional expenditures which will be made for unemployment insurance as a result of the extension of these benefits to more people and for longer periods. Here alone the additional cost will be $200 million more than in 1956-57.
I should like the Minister of Labour to explain where this $200 million in extra unemployment benefits came from. I should like the Minister of Labour to explain when he speaks, if he will do me the honour of giving me some attention while I am referring to him, what the Prime Minister could have meant when he said that $200 million more in unemployment insurance benefits were paid in the last two years than in the year 1956-57. If that figure is correct-perhaps it is correct; the minister will be able to check us on that-and if that additional amount of money was paid out for which the Prime Minister takes credit to his government, it was paid out because there were unprecedented levels of unemployment which
Supply-Labour
required these payments. However, to make a virtue of that is a very strange thing indeed.
Perhaps the minister will also confirm my statement that if this figure of $200 million is accurate as representing benefits received from the government, according to the Prime Minister, 80 per cent of these benefits came from the pockets of the employers and employees. It is a very strange kind of political advertising that takes credit to a government for contributions made by the employers and the employees to the insurance benefits of the unemployed employees.
Last night I also mentioned the strange statement of the Prime Minister in this strange speech-perhaps the minister will also deal with this when he replies-that our gross national product had increased 3 per cent last year. I pointed out last night, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister was only $160 million out in that figure on the basis of his own method of calculation. If he had adopted the method of calculation put forward by the Minister of Finance when he estimated the gross national product, that is a calculation which is based on stable prices and takes into consideration price increases, the Prime Minister would have been over $700 million out in his statement.
These are some of the matters which perhaps can be dealt with by the minister in the discussion of this item of the estimates, but there is one other reference I should like to make before I sit down. He will know, of course, that when I spoke on this item some days ago I addressed to the government through him some general questions on labour policy and unemployment policy. The hon. member for Trinity also put forward some suggestions which I thought were very interesting and constructive. We on this side are often charged by the government with not putting forward constructive proposals but when the minister replies at the close of the discussion of this item of the estimates, or whenever he feels like replying, we expect him to deal with the particular suggestions which have been put on the record.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can assure the minister that I will not be very long. However, I should like to bring a number of matters to his attention. The first is that as our urban areas grow in population it is only natural that the staff of the unemployment insurance commission should also grow. It does not take long in terms of years for an office that had 15 or 20 employees to increase to 60 or more employees, not only because the increase in unemployment is a problem but also because of the growth in population. At this time I should like to make

Supply-Labour
the plea again that as much as possible, and in line with efficiency and the maximum output in these offices, the minister make every effort to keep the offices on as small a unit basis as he can.
I know that the officers of his department naturally like promotions, and as the offices grow so does their rank and their income as civil servants. Therefore each and every time the minister looks into the possibility of opening another office the advice he receives from his officers is usually against opening such additional offices because it affects their own position and income. There is a tendency for the officials to continue to advise the minister not to grant requests for the opening of additional offices.
This is of particular concern to those of us who live in rapidly growing urban areas. As population grows and as the need arises we hope the minister will understand the position and will agree a little more readily than he has in the past to the establishment of additional offices of the unemployment insurance commission. I do not like to see men become mere cogs in a machine, and when you have very large offices handling thousands of men a week I believe we make mere cogs in a machine out of men. So far as obtaining employment for people is concerned, I think this cause would be better served if there were offices in the local communities which would be aware of employment openings that might exist. They would be more aware of possible employment openings than a major office with a large hierarchy of civil servants. I also believe there would be more humane treatment of those who are unemployed and must use the facilities of these offices.
I have in mind particularly such expanding municipalities as are found around the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster. There are municipalities around New Westminster with a population three or four times that of the little city of New Westminster. Yet the unemployed in these surrounding municipalities must have their unemployment insurance needs attended to in the New Westminster unemployment insurance office, which is already larger than it needs to be in order to render efficient advice and help to the unemployed. Naturally the same criticism applies to the unemployment insurance offices in the city of Vancouver. I do not believe the government should sponsor the establishment of ever larger institutions when the matter of dealing with the needs of our unemployed is involved.
Another plea I should like to make at this time is that the minister use his influence
fMr. Regier.]
in the government to obtain much more money for the retraining of workers. We will never be relieved of the problem of unemployment as long as automation is with us, and I do not see the end of automation and its effects. I believe the minister will agree that as the years go by more and more money will have to be spent on retraining our workers.
In so far as a large number of them are concerned, we will have to make arrangements whereby we pay them a maintenance allowance while they are being re-educated in order to enable them to take other employment. It is very difficult for a man with a family to agree to attend a training course for six months or more if he has no regular income. The day may well have arrived when the government, through the medium of the unemployment insurance commission, ought to give serious consideration to the payment of a living allowance to those of our unemployed who want to obtain the education necessary to take other employment.
I should like at this time to appeal to the minister to take measures very early in the year directed toward launching the next winter works program. I believe the minister now wishes that he had begun these projects a little earlier last year. I think the time is now when initial moves should be made whereby we could have a vastly expanded and enlarged winter works program next year. I hope when the minister begins planning next year's winter works program he will devise ways and means whereby the municipalities do not have to assume such very heavy obligations in order to supply a limited number of men with work. The minister indicated some months or more ago how pleased he was with the fact that some 38 per cent of the money that was being expended was being used to pay wages.
I have statistics here to show what happened in Burnaby. I note that the headline on the article from the British Columbian of April 16, 1959 says, "Winter Works Bring $72,000 From Ottawa". It says:
Burnaby has spent $300,000 of the $557,720 allotted to eight public works projects that qualify for federal winter works financial aid.
Of this $557,720, the federal government is paying $71,926. This means that the municipality of Burnaby, in order to supply employment to roughly 100 men, had to go into debt to the tune of almost half a million dollars for these undertakings. If we are going to try to solve our unemployment problems in this manner it is my contention that we are going to break every municipal

government in Canada. The municipalities simply cannot afford to go out and borrow money, especially with interest rates as they are now, to the extent of $500,000 for every 100 men who must be supplied with employment. Our municipalities simply are not able to assume that kind of burden.
I should like, therefore, to propose that the minister attempt to persuade his colleagues in the government that when next year's winter works program is launched the municipalities be assured that the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act will be reactivated. This act is on the statute books, and under it the government has authority to give aid to the municipalities.
This act, which was introduced in the thirties, was specifically designed to provide employment through municipal organizations. I know the capital which is available under it is limited. However, the government might easily ask parliament to expand the capitalization allowed. I believe the present capitalization is $30 million, but in the light of Canadian problems and costs of today I think the minister would agree that our municipalities might easily use something in the nature of $300 million.
This act was a means whereby loans for self-liquidating projects were made available to municipalities at a very nominal rate of interest. I believe that if next year's winter works program is to be a success this act will have to be reactivated so these low cost loans are available to the municipalities, or the government will have to find other ways and means whereby the municipalities will not have to go into debt to the extent of half a million dollars in order to supply employment to 100 men for the five winter months.
The other proposal I have concerns the annuities branch. I know the minister is very much interested in the cause of labour. I know that he has heard much about industrial pension plans. I know the minister knows quite a number of the disadvantages of the present industrial pension plan arrangements, especially when a worker leaves one place of employment, either through no fault of his own or otherwise, and moves to another place of employment. The worker usually loses his pension rights in such instances. Once he reaches a certain age he has a difficult time in obtaining employment because he is told that for pension purposes he is too old.
I should like the minister to have the annuities branch look into the possibilities of establishing, under the annuities branch, a portable pension plan for Canadian workers. I feel that the annuities branch could be augmented and expanded in a manner which
Supply-Labour
would give employers and unions some encouragement to transfer their present pension arrangements into the government annuities branch. If they did that they would then be making a move toward the establishment of a portable pension plan for Canadian workers.
Many members in the house have made remarks about industrial unrest. We have often heard the blame placed on organized labour. Well, all of us regret industrial unrest. However, it is sometimes part of the system. Unless we want to establish a dictatorship I do not see how, under our present concept of liberty, industrial unrest can be avoided. However, I feel that there has been a lot of exaggeration in this regard. I should like to place on the record a limited number of remarks made in the legislature of British Columbia by Rae Eddie, M.L.A. for New Westminster. I read these as they were reproduced in the B. C. Lumber Worker, the first issue in March, 1959. Mr. Eddie was pointing out very effectively that strike losses are being magnified and are not as harmful as many people would have us believe.
He says the facts are these. He used March, 1958 as a sample because he says that was the month in which labour disputes were particularly heavy in British Columbia. He says the figures show that out of total man days lost, 86 per cent of that time was lost through unemployment and 13 per cent was lost through illness, leaving less than 1 per cent of man days lost because of labour disputes. In short, unemployment cost more than 95 times as much as did strikes in time loss, and illness cost 15 times as much. To me that does not sound like irresponsible use of a free man's right to use his ultimate bargaining weapon.
We in this house are greatly concerned about the growing needs of government in the way of revenue. The other day we had a proposition that would cost several hundred million dollars. However, may I say in conclusion that our present level of unemployment, with half a million unemployed in Canada, over a period of one year means a loss in wealth that has not been produced of $1,500 million. That is, $1J billion of wealth is lost in one year because of unemployment. That wealth is more than the cost of all family allowances, old age pensions and many other welfare enterprises added together. The cost of unemployment to the Canadian economy is today by far the greatest cost that the people of Canada are paying for having voted as they did in March of last year.

I am now making a suggestion that will bring business to the employment office. The matter concerns government contracts. My criticism or observation will apply equally to other ridings in Canada where there are government contracts. I suggest to the minister that he consult with the Minister of Public Works and see to it that there is inserted in the contracts awarded by the government a clause to the effect that the labourers shall be drawn from that section of the country in which the contract has been awarded.
At the present time the situation in Pembroke or in the district is that the number of unemployed is about 2,500. This situation is extremely serious. If the contractors and the subcontractors as well-particularly the subcontractors-would draw their labour from the section of the community in which they have the contract, there would be considerable alleviation of the distress in my section of the country. I would ask the minister if he would discuss this matter with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and with the Minister of Public Works and ascertain whether there cannot be inserted in these tenders and in the contracts when they are finally signed a clause to the effect that the labour shall be drawn, as far as possible, from the section of the country in which the contract is to be carried out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
The other evening, Mr. Chairman, when we were discussing other matters concerning the Department of Labour it was not found possible, because of the rules of the house, to discuss certain matters which the opposition desired to discuss at that time. While I have no intention of repeating what I said in the debate then, there are however some things that I believe should be put on the record.
I have, of course, no complaint to make with regard to the ruling of the Chair by which all members of the house must abide. It is because of that desire on my part and on the part of all of us who sit here that we follow the decisions of His Honour the Speaker. The ruling was that anything having to do with the reasons for non-compliance with the statute should not then have been discussed. The statute, of course, is the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is why at this time I feel that I should put certain matters on Hansard which I was prevented from doing on the earlier occasion.
[Mr. Forgie.l
At the time I indicated that there were, on the part of the minister, certain violations. Perhaps that word was too strong; perhaps I should have used another term. Perhaps I should have said that the minister had not abided by the terms of the statute. But whether it is one term or the other that is used, I do not think it makes any difference in the effect.
There are two or three points in which I am interested. One of them is the report of August 26, 1958, which the minister tabled at the request of the hon. member for Essex East. My purpose at this time is to say that this report forms part of sessional paper 82A and should be incorporated therein by reference. My purpose in saying that is found in section 89 (1) of the statute which can be divided under two heads, and which reads in part as follows:
(1)	Within four months after the end of each fiscal year the advisory committee shall make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the fund-
Furthermore, over and above that obligation, the advisory committee may report at any time it sees fit, as I take it was its intention in the report of August 26, 1958. I have particular reference at this time to the paragraph in the beginning of this report which reads as follows:
In the meantime we respectfully draw your attention to our report of July 18, 1958.
My contention, Mr. Chairman, is that legally the moment the advisory committee, in any report to the minister, puts in a clause of this nature, then by reference any additional report is incorporated into the report required to be made under this statute. It then falls to the minister under section 90 (2) to lay that report on the table of the house. Section 90 (2) reads as follows:
(2)	The minister shall lay every report made under section 89 before parliament within thirty days after it was submitted to the governor in council, or if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first thirty days thereafter that parliament is sitting.
I say that the words "submitted to the governor in council" should be read with reference to the whole statute. My contention, with great deference, is that both these documents should have been tabled in accordance with section 90, subsection 2.
I think too, sir, that there has been an infraction, an evasion, of the statute in that section 19 (1) has not been complied with, because there is not now legally in existence an unemployment insurance advisory committee. I think that has been made quite clear in an earlier debate and I need not repeat it on this occasion. But because of the circumstances in which the committee finds

itself three members have found it necessary to hand in their resignations. Therefore that committee, because it does not consist of the required number of members, which shall be not less than six nor more than eight, does not legally exist.
Then, of course, there is the fact that there has been an infraction of this statute in its intention. I did mention this matter the other evening and I will not repeat it now except in passing. I would ask the minister if he will not tell the committee under what power he requested certain information and a report from the advisory committee. As I look at this act, and look at it as fairly as I can, there is a clear cut section, 91 (1), which gives the governor in council that power and that authority, but I see nowhere in the act any authority to the minister to act in the way he did.
In addition there is the unfortunate situation which exists between the minister and the labour movement at the present time. I say to the minister, with all the regard I have for him, that I am afraid he must assume full responsibility for this unfortunate situation, because in my modest estimation I believe he failed to carry out the required consultation with labour. I listened very carefully to the statement the minister made in defence of his position, but as I read section 19 (2) it is clearly set out therein that at least one of the members of the advisory committee other than the chairman shall be appointed after consultation with organizations representative of workers and an equal number, after consultation with organizations, representative of employers.
As a result of the failure of the minister to comply with that very clear and important provision in our legislation, the two most important labour unions have stated that they do not recognize the representative of the minister or of the government as their representative on the commission. The commission will therefore be composed of two government appointees and one representing employers. Although the minister may claim that the recent appointment does not constitute a technical violation of the act, I am sure he cannot deny that he did not comply with the spirit and the intention of this legislative provision in that respect.
As a result of that clear violation by the minister and the government of the spirit of the legislation, the three representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress and of the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour on the unemployment insurance advisory committee have announced their resignations. There was no other course, I believe, for these men to adopt under the circumstances. Indeed, in addition to those specific
Supply-Labour
and important responsibilities which are contained in the act, the advisory committee must work in close collaboration with the commission. Since the labour movement cannot feel that it is properly represented on the commission, as it has the right to be so represented, its representatives could not continue to act as members of the advisory committee and to work with the commission. The minister, I am afraid, must assume the ultimate responsibility for those resignations and for the situation which, as I indicated, is in contravention of section 19 subsection 2 of the act, which clearly states that at least one member of the advisory committee must represent labour.
As a consequence of these three recent resignations, the advisory committee has at present only five members other than the chairman. Moreover, it is doubtful whether there is at present on the committee a member who has been "appointed after consultation with organizations representative of workers" in accordance with the section to which I have referred. The minister-

I am sure that no one would agree with that statement more quickly than the minister; but under the circumstances, willingly or not, voluntarily or involuntarily, he did not con-

Supply-Labour
ciliate in this case. True, he gave the house an explanation of what happened, but that explanation is contradicted by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, and clearly contradicted. It is contradicted, too, by the three representatives who handed in their resignations. Therefore I think I am safe and accurate in saying, first of all, that the advisory committee has no legal status as it stands today; and second, with all respect to the minister, I do not think he used his conciliatory powers or facilities in the manner in which they should have been used on the occasion.
I do not want to go into this unduly and pursue the matter ad nauseam, but I think there is one point which I must make and that has to do with the Quebec representative on that body, Mr. Jean Marchand, who is the representative or the secretary of the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. The minister, and again I say this to him with deference, stated that Mr. Jean Marchand was official affiliated to a political party which was not the Progressive Conservative party. That I submit is not an accurate statement. That is not a fact, and I challenge the minister to substantiate that accusation. Why should the minister have made that statement, if it is not in accordance with the fact? I have no doubt that Mr. Marchand is not in that position. If he were I am sure he could not hold the position which he holds at the present time. I am prompted to say that it might be because of the position Mr. Marchand held during the strike of the employees of the C.B.C. that the minister was prompted to make that statement. Be that as it may, I do not think the statement was accurate; I do not think it should have been made, and I do not think there is any foundation for it.

The hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet may know of these facts, whereas I have no such information. I am, however, convinced that the minister's statement in this house was not in accordance with the facts and that, under the circumstances, he should not have made it because to my mind it is a responsibility

of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to reconcile the various attitudes instead of confusing them, as he attempted to do.
Furthermore, if I may say so, Mr. Chairman, without in the least wishing to cast reflections on the Minister of Labour, I think the attitude shown by Mr. Jean Marchand in the C.B.C. producers' strike had a great deal to do with the attitude taken by the government towards him.
That is the reason why I made my statement a moment ago. Now, if I may return to the point I was trying to make-and I was trying to make it as calmly as possible in the circumstances, and I am sure the minister accepts it in that light -I was trying to point out that the minister failed to consult, in accordance with section 19 (2) of the act, the various labour organizations when the appointment of Mr. MacArthur was made, and that because of this failure an unfortunate situation has arisen as between the minister and the labour movement, a situation which I believe has led to the worsening of the relationship between the two.
I am sure the minister himself would be the first to recognize the need and importance of close and continued collaboration between himself and the labour movement for the proper and effective operation and administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The point now arises, how does the minister propose to secure this essential collaboration? When and how does he intend to extricate himself from the difficult, delicate and awkward position in which he finds himself? How does he intend to get out of the illegal position which exists today?
A moment ago the minister said he expected to appoint persons in lieu of the three who had resigned. No one can anticipate, of course, what the appointments will be, but will they be truly representatives of labour? Will they be appointed after consultation with labour? These are questions which I am sure cannot be answered at this time. So I conclude this part of my remarks by stating that in my opinion a serious mistake has been made because of the fact

that there was a failure to consult and because there was a failure to conciliate. This has set a bad standard for both employers and employees. I trust and hope that this situation will be rectified.
Before I resume my seat I would like to make a suggestion. I can speak only for myself, but the suggestion is this; that item 1 of the minister's estimates be allowed to stand, after the discussion thereof has been terminated, and that meantime we continue with the other items of the department in order that we may get from the minister a report on the winter works program. I make this suggestion with deference. I think it will hasten the consideration of the estimates, because I have a feeling that if this were done we could certainly dispose of these additional items very quickly.
