speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in opening my brief remarks may I congratulate the minister for his opening remarks on the presentation of his estimates and say that I welcomed the announcement of consideration for older workers. I believe the minister well knows this is a subject of great interest to me as well as to many hon. members on both sides of this chamber. I am sure many were gratified to hear that steps were being taken to find a solution to the problem confronting older workers in Canada. I have spoken on this subject on previous occasions and do not wish to elaborate further on the point at the present time.
I wish to bring to the minister's attention the need for a change in the regulations at some future time. It may be, of course, that the objections I raise to the present regulations could be met by valid arguments, but I would hope the minister and his officials might give the matter some reconsideration. I refer to the regulations under section 172, subsection 3, paragraph (b) of the act. The regulations came into effect last autumn, I believe, and as a result the following notice was distributed through national employment offices to a number of people applying for unemployment insurance. The notice is specifically directed to farmers, and the pertinent part reads:
All earning must be declared (see paragraph 15 of "Information for Claimants" form 501D). This includes earnings from farm operations.
If you dispose of any farm produce (milk, grain, livestock, etc.) during a week for which you are claiming benefit you must include as earnings for that week one-half of the amount of money that you received or will receive as a result of the transaction.
The notice then goes on to make some reference to penalties. This has no reference to the point I should like to make. Just after the end of the last war we all know that the Department of Veterans Affairs under the Veterans' Land Act encouraged veterans to purchase small holdings of land, up to four, five or six acres or whatever it was, for the purpose of assisting the veteran and his family to become more or less self-sufficient. This was one of the purposes in any event. This policy was to assist those who became unemployed. They were encouraged to get

Supply-Labour
a few chickens, pigs or cows, and generally one might say veterans were encouraged to put their money into projects of this kind.
Nowadays many people among the farm population work in the cities and there are many persons who because of high tax rates in certain urban areas have bought small holdings out in the country. Their wives may keep a few chickens or they may keep some pigs or possibly even one or two beef cattle or a cow or something of that nature. This trend is becoming increasingly common.
If an individual is able to save some money which he invests in real estate and draws rent from his investment he is in no way affected by the regulations to which I referred. Neither is he penalized if he invests his money in stocks, bonds or securities. However, if an individual invests his money in any kind of farming operation from which he draws income he is penalized under this section of the act. I cannot help but feel this is a form of discrimination against those workers who live in rural areas and have invested their money in small holdings of land from which they draw a little income.
I know that one of the arguments in favour of the present regulations is that investment in real estate or stocks and bonds represents a consolidation of the past labours of the individual, and if they draw income from this source it is not considered as earnings. I realize that it is sometimes difficult to draw a fine line in matters of this kind, but I have difficulty in comprehending the difference between a person who has invested money in real estate which he has to repair and maintain and from which he draws income in the form of rent, and a person who on the other hand has invested in a small holding of land from which he draws some income through keeping a few chickens, pigs or something of that nature which he must feed whether or not he is working elsewhere. In the former case the individual is not affected by this section of the act but in the latter case the individual is penalized.
I believe these regulations would even go so far as to make necessary the declaration of money received by an individual from the sale of a cow, for instance, which he sold in order to purchase another cow. This is clearly capital, but he would have to declare the money he received from the sale and would be penalized as a result. I appreciate that it is difficult to administer some of the provisions in the act but I would hope that the minister and his officials would give some reconsideration to this matter.
My next remarks relate to what I have just said. Because of interrelated activities in our

economy today often there is a very fine distinction between city workers, those who are half working in the city and half in rural areas, and farmers. In other words there are no clearly defined black and whites but we have an increasing number of grays somewhere in the middle today. I refer to the distinction between industrial workers and farmers which used to be more clearly defined. Because of this I suggest to the minister that he might give consideration to appointing someone to the unemployment insurance advisory committee who has at least some knowledge of farm problems and can represent the views of people who may have small holdings in rural areas but who may work in a factory in the city. I feel that this is important, and I urge the minister to give consideration to this suggestion.
In conclusion may I say that in my opinion and in the opinion of many people throughout the country with whom I have discussed these matters the present Minister of Labour is probably the best minister of labour this country has ever had. I believe this view must be recognized by hon. gentlemen opposite. In fact the only conclusion to which I can come is that hon. members of the official opposition and the C.C.F. are becoming alarmed at the popularity of the Minister of Labour in the country. I am quite certain of this in view of recent speeches that have been made in this house, which cannot be interpreted in any way other than as attempts to tear down the excellent reputation the minister has acquired for himself, and very justifiably so.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been asked to bring certain complaints to the attention of the house and the minister by a good number of trade unionists in my constituency, a number of members of the Canadian Legion and some business people. I have also received considerable correspondence along the same line. In the national employment service we have a very excellent organization that provides an opportunity for employers to register their employment needs and for employees to register for employment. From my contact with the service I would say that generally speaking they are doing a very good job, sometimes under quite difficult circumstances.
As opposed to that we have the immigration department also undertaking the responsibility of seeking employment for immigrants. I am not criticizing the officials of the immigration department. They are undertaking their duties as they are supposed to according to the act and the regulations and their instructions. However, people to whom I have spoken think this creates an unnecessary

duplication of expenditure and a certain unfairness to Canadian citizens, and that the procedures create quite unnecessary ill feeling at certain times.
I have personal knowledge of an immigration officer who in some cases travels two or three hundred miles to find employment for immigrants. I am not blaming the immigrant who naturally wants to get employment. In fact this officer travels even greater distances on occasion. Funds are provided which give him the opportunity of travelling all over the district, visiting small places, quizzing employers and in some cases obtaining employment where the employer did not consider that he really needed an employee for the work in question. They are pretty thorough in that respect in going into every nook and corner of the Kootenays and trying to find employment for immigrants.
One or two managers of small lumber companies have mentioned to me how efficient the immigration officials are in that respect, in that they have suggested that the employer put the man on for a week or two even if he cannot provide work for very long. The immigration official says he has to get jobs for the immigrants somehow and that it will be a great help to him if the employer can give the man a job, and so on and so on.
The officials of the national employment service do not have the same opportunity. I know the local managers do what they can, within close range of the towns in which employment offices are situated, to come in contact with employers quite frequently, but the funds available and their duties are such as to make it impossible for them to travel the district in the same way as the officers of the immigration department. During recent years I have had it repeatedly brought to my attention by the people I have mentioned that there has been a certain unfairness.
I want to cite one case, which could be repeated many times. This man came to see me personally, having been sent to me by the secretary of the Legion branch and the secretary of his trade union. This man was born in a town in my constituency. He served overseas for six years in the second world war and had a very commendable record. He now has four children and had been unemployed for five months when he came to see me. He is an electrician and there was no employment in sight. An immigrant came into the district who was an electrician, was in the town one day and got a job because the immigration official just happened to arrive at a certain place at the right time, when the employer was about to notify the national employment service that they needed an electrician.
Supply-Labour
The criticisms of these people are quite sound that there is unnecessary duplication, and at times this brings about criticism of the national employment service which is not justified. I have heard people complain about the national employment service officials not getting out and rustling up jobs, and I have had to explain over and over again that they do not have the same opportunity because there is no financial provision and their duties will not permit it.
I could illustrate this complaint with a number of similar cases, but I will only refer to the one case. With respect to my own experience, may I say that after receiving complaints I am in the habit of investigating because I like to get the facts, and as a result of the complaints I have received and my personal experience I suggest that the registration of jobs and the seeking of employment should be the sole responsibility of the national employment service. All this work should come under one branch. In addition, there should be provision for appropriate officials of the offices to travel around the districts in order to visit employers in the same way that immigration officers now do. In that way it would be fairer to Canadian citizens and fairer to immigrants. They would not encounter these unnecessary hostilities which are very easily built up, particularly in small communities.
I have gone to considerable pains on two or three occasions to dampen the fires of resentment which were directed at the time at the national employment service and also at the poor immigrant in question because of the method of doing things at the present time. I have brought these views of my constituents to the attention of the minister, and I hope serious consideration will be given to some consolidation of the services that I have dealt with so briefly.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Laurier is extremely important. He has asked the Minister of Labour to allow the first item to stand so we will have some opportunity at a later date to ascertain what is likely to be the government's policy for attacking unemployment next fall and winter. The minister has indicated that he cannot accept the suggestion; consequently we are going to observe the traditional routine of dealing with these estimates. That is the responsibility of the minister, and apart from disagreeing with him for the reasons stated by the hon. member for Laurier I do not quarrel with his decision. But we therefore have an obligation to ask the government at this time what its policy with regard to unemployment is going to be for the ensuing period.

Supply-Labour
The minister understandably has taken some pride in the achievements under his winter work program. The program I am talking about is not the advertising campaign urging people to provide employment. Without belittling the value of that, though recognizing that it really has not cut very deeply, what I am referring to is the winter work program which involves contributions by the federal government together with the provinces to municipally conceived projects. The minister has said that obviously the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier are to be construed as an approbation of that program, and in understandable modesty the Minister of Labour says he is very glad to know that hon. gentlemen on this side approve the program and share his pride in its achievements.
I think the Minister of Labour is under a great misapprehension. We on this side of the house welcome the program in so far as it goes. Any program designed to assist men and women who are out of work to And gainful employment will receive our support, but the minister does not do justice to the record of debate this session when he suggests that we are satisfied with the program. We are not. This program was announced in the fall of last year but it was ill timed, and as a result was not capable of the productive results which it otherwise would have had. What we are now saying is that while we all hope there will be a real improvement in the unemployment picture, there are indices that suggest it is going to be a serious problem, though we hope however not on the same level as last year. Every indication would appear to support the view that unemployment nevertheless will be present with us next fall and winter.
What we are asking the government to do is not wait until Christmas or late fall to declare its policy, but to tell the country and the house now what its policy is going to be. Is this program going to continue? If it is going to continue, the municipalities ought to be told far enough ahead of time so they can make the necessary preparations through budgetary arrangements, through use of necessary facilities, personnel and the like to cope with the problem. The minister takes credit for this program. I think he is overstating the case when we recognize that as of the last reported period there were some 525,000 people without jobs, and that the number of unplaced applicants had increased by almost 4,000.
This is a picture that does not warrant the suggestion that we can coast along as the government has coasted along, during the past 18 months. Now we would like to know from the minister, has all the money that was voted for this particular project

been expended by the government? How many people have been put to work? When we are told how many people have been put to work under this program, we realize its limitations. The fact that 33,000 or 40,000 people have been put to work as a result of this program is in itself commendable, but it is nothing compared to the problem of unemployment that faces the country at the present time. I do not believe the minister is on sound ground when he takes great satisfaction from these figures, in the light of the total unemployment problem and in the light of the very limited achievements of this program of works.
Now, what we want to know is, what is the government now doing-

Do you want us to drop this
program?

My hon. friend
does not do himself justice. Of course we do not want him to drop this program. What I want him to do is announce this program at a time when the municipalities can prepare for it. Tell us now, are you going to embark on this program next year?

The hon. member talks about
the preparation of budgets by municipalities. I think I should advise him that the municipalities have already set their budgets for this year, and a new budget will not be set until after the new year, in 1960. Budgets, therefore, have nothing to do with it.
Oh, no.
Ontario is not the whole country.

I have had some experience in this connection. Preparation for any plan of this nature at this time would be a little premature. We will have to look at the situation later on to see what the position may be this winter. I realize the plan could have been announced a little earlier last winter, but there was no harm done by the announcement being made when it was. In the first week of this plan we received over 500 applications.
Now, most certainly, if it is found necessary later on this year that this program should be continued for another year, the experience we have gained during this winter will help us in deciding earlier, and the plan will be announced earlier

there is no question about that-if it is decided to go ahead with it.

I thank the minister for incorporating my remarks in his. I believe he has only confirmed now what I have said. He has said that municipal budgets are already prepared. Of course he knows that is not the case nationally. As

a matter of fact on December 23 last the minister made a statement which confirms what I have just been saying. The minister said that the interest shown to date in this program and the favourable reception to it from municipalities all across the country are very encouraging, and this was particularly true since budgetary restrictions have prevented many municipalities from submitting projects until their 1959 works programs are approved by the newly elected councils.
This is surely an indication of the truth of my statements. My own city of Windsor is a pretty good illustration of the weakness of this program. Shortly after the program was announced last year we met under the capable direction of that devoted public servant Mr. John Sharrer, the director of the unemployment insurance offices in Windsor. The members of parliament, members of the legislature, representatives of the unions and of management met to discuss this particular program and ascertain whether it would be adaptable to the situation in Windsor. The mayor and the council of Windsor indicated that they could not participate in this program because their budgetary plans were already drawn up, and also, to use the language of the former controller, Mrs. Montrose, because the plan was inadequate in that it did not provide financial assistance from the two senior levels of government in connection with supplies.
I am sure my hon. friend knows as well as I do that if he wants to bring in a works program that is really going to put thousands of people to work, the federal share should be extended beyond merely assisting in direct employment. It has to encourage projects, and one way of encouraging projects will be for the federal and provincial governments to do more than merely share the cost of labour involved in those projects. In my own city of Windsor, where there has been heavy unemployment, we have not been able to take advantage of this program. I think the fact that in the province of Ontario this program has not put more than-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-9,000 or 10,000 to work-
-over 11,000 people to work, in a province of 6 million people-
But this program was not designed to put everybody to work.

-is a pretty good indication of the failure of this program. We admit that this type of program is valuable. What we are asking the minister to do is to announce, at the earliest possible date,
Supply-Labour
whether or not the program is to be continued; that is what we asked last year.
I promised the hon. member that the date would be announced at the earliest possible time.
Will the minister say that this program to cope with unemployment will be announced before we rise at the end of June or the middle of July? Will the minister promise us that?
A decision will have to be made in the light of the situation in the month of August.
My hon. friend says the month of August, but parliament will not be sitting. We were caught that way last year. The Leader of the Opposition, in the month of June-
We asked for it in August last year.
You did not know about it in August.

The Leader of the Opposition, in the months of June and August, asked the Minister of Labour if he did not think that in view of the outlook for the fall and winter the government should take steps to do something about combatting unemployment. That request was supported by members of the opposition. Nothing was done between August and the time when, a week or so before the Prime Minister left the country, he announced the program in Saskatoon.
At a provincial convention.

Yes, at a provincial convention. We do not want to be caught in the same situation, because we have had a very serious level of unemployment this year. Many thousands of people have suffered as a result. Having promised to do something about unemployment, this government owes to the unemployed and to this parliament the obligation to tell us, before we leave, what are its plans to meet unemployment next fall and winter.
I just want to repeat to the hon. member what I said earlier, namely that the responsibility for action in this matter rests with the government and we are assuming that responsibility.
Parliament does not matter.

I am sure I understand my hon. friend's difficulty. I know that if he were left alone and were the only minister in the government he would announce today that this program was going to be continued, and that its features would be

Supply-Labour
refined and liberalized so it could be more effective. But I am not addressing myself only to the minister; I am addressing myself to all the members of the government who have the obligation of sharing with him the responsibility for action. Surely we are entitled to know, before this session closes, whether the municipalities can now start preparing programs that will at least put this same number to work, if not more. But if the hon. gentleman waits, as I am afraid it is his intention, not until August, September or October but until November, we shall have a recurrence of this same situation; and a year from now we shall be arguing in this house, just as we are arguing at this moment, and criticising the government for not having taken in the middle of 1959 preparatory steps to meet a situation in late 1959 and the winter of 1960. That is the reason for the proposal made by the hon. member for Laurier. It was made for the purpose of assisting the minister in the passage of his estimates and at the same time preserving-as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out a moment ago-the rights of parliament, in its right to ascertain government policy with regard to the most serious problem that confronts us in Canada at this time, namely that of unemployment. This government owes to this parliament and to this country, more than any other government in the history of Canada, action along these lines because this government made a solemn commitment to the unemployed of our nation as no other government has ever done. For that reason the government should not hesitate to give us now a clear indication of its policy.
The hon. member for Trinity the other day outlined a program which, if adopted, would put many thousands of people to work. What is the government's attitude with regard to that program? Does it accept what the hon. member for Trinity suggested? Does it think his suggestion had any merit? This is the opportunity for the Minister of Labour to tell us. If he does not, we can only conclude that this government is going to run a calculated risk and trust that there will be no unemployment of a serious nature next year. In running it, it runs the risk of adding, unwittingly or wittlingly, to the continued discomfort and distress of thousands of people.

Mr. Chairman, every time I rise to speak I always seem to be doing so against the clock. However, that may be a good thing. I did not intend to speak at this stage, but this morning I received from one of my constituents a letter which has

prompted me to do so. I should like to read a portion of this letter. It reads in part as follows:
Dear Doug.:
This morning's headlines are "steady workers to pay more employment insurance". Surely you can help to curb this. For 11 years I have worked for my boss and paid employment insurance. If I stop, I will get one year of insurance benefits that will not keep me happy. Why can't we have as the U.S.A. have, the security plan, forced saving that all comes back to the worker? After all, it is my money. I have already paid taxes. Why should the "steady" worker keep the numbers happy who never stay on a job longer than possible?
To me, Mr. Chairman, that letter indicates that there is some feeling of dissatisfaction among these workers who are steadily employed. They understandably feel that the money they have paid into the fund is theirs and that they are being penalized by virtue of being steady employees.
In order to remove this feeling of dissatisfaction may I make the following proposal to the Minister of Labour. Can some consideration be given to protecting the unemployment insurance fund by making the contributions of the employee payable to his estate if the contributor never draws on the fund? The estate created by his contributions might be a very modest one, but I think such a procedure might give some people the incentive to build up their contributions instead of thinking of ways and means of depleting the fund at every opportunity.
If such a plan were adopted the contributor would feel that his contributions would be a sort of savings fund. Even if the estate were a modest one I think it might be of some assistance to those in the lower income brackets who, after all, make up the larger number of people who pay into this fund. It might be of some comfort to the older workers who would know that some extra money is coming to their family if anything happens to them. By limiting the amount payable to the estate of the contributor to the actual contributions paid by him we could emphasize to him that it was his fund and that he is not being-if I may use the word-cheated out of his own money.
The minister may see disadvantages in my proposal. I have not spoken about it at great length because I can appreciate the tremendous administrative problems that would arise from such a scheme. However, I make this proposal because I think some consideration should be given to removing this understandable feeling which some of the people have that they are being unjustly penalized.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, you will recall that prior to the adjournment of this morning's session I had submitted a proposal to the Minister of Labour. This proposal was that in order to remove the feeling prevalent among many that those who are steadily employed subsidize those who are out of work, the contributions paid into the unemployment insurance fund by the steadily employed worker should be made payable to his estate.
I do not intend to repeat the remarks which I made this morning, and I shall conclude by saying that, in my opinion, such a scheme would not only make the contributor feel that he was really protecting his contributions to the extent that he will get all his money back if he has never drawn on the fund, but also I think that such a plan would slow the drain on the unemployment insurance fund because it would encourage people not to use their unemployment insurance benefits unless they really had to. This may be a very difficult plan to implement, and if I may be permitted to say so this is a very ambitious project. However, if the minister does not feel that this project can be implemented at this time, then I would urge that the government consider this plan on a broader basis so it will ultimately tie in with a national program of social security.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of delaying the passing of the estimates of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), but at the request of the Catholic and Canadian trade unions of Joliette, I should like to ask the minister to consider the possibility of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act in view of the fact that certain large categories of workers are not yet receiving the benefits and protection provided by the legislation. The Unemployment Insurance Act should be amended so that the benefits it provides might extend to workers in hospital and religious institutions. All that would be required would be to delete section 27 d and e of the said legislation.
Again at the request of farmers in the federal riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm, and more especially cigar and cigarette
Supply-Labour
tobacco growers, I must say it would be of paramount importance that the minister consider the possibility of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, as soon as possible in order to make its benefits available to farm workers. So far, I have received many delegations of farmers from my riding who are having a hard time finding the farm help they need to operate successfully. I know that the government is looking into the possibility of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act and of making it easier for farmers to hire farm hands by allowing such workers to qualify for the benefits provided by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I admit that the administration of the legislation would be very difficult and complicated. It might be important, perhaps, to consider as soon as possible the possibility of extending the provisions of the act to farmers who grow special crops, such as producers of cigar or cigarette tobacco.
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the Minister of Labour, as usual, will look into the possibility of introducing the necessary amendments so that farm workers may enjoy the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I have several different topics I wish to say something about with regard to the first item of the labour estimates. First of all, I would like to say something about the winter works program following along the line taken the other day by my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo. In that context I would like to draw some attention again, as has been done once or twice before, to the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo about these municipal winter works projects, which answer is to be found in Hansard of April 22 at page 2928.
I am not going over the details of all these figures, but if they are compared, as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo compared them, with the latest available figures for unemployment in the different provinces and regions of this country, it will be found that this winter works program is effective in almost precisely inverse proportion to unemployment. This 50-50 arrangement has this effect in this field, as it unhappily has in so many others, that it follows the text: To him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.
That is particularly true in the case of the province, one constituency of which has done

Supply-Labour
me the honour of electing me to this parliament. It will be seen that unemployment in that province, according to the latest figures which the minister gave us, was very substantially higher than in any other part of Canada. The reasons for that have been given before and I am not going to go into them in greater detail now, except to say one thing. As the minister knows, there was a disastrous situation in the fisheries of Newfoundland last year, the kind of disaster which I am sure, if it had happened in any other province, would have been relieved by this parliament.
For some reason or other, however, despite the fact that it was brought to the attention of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Fisheries in October before the date on which this winter works program was first announced at a political convention in Saskatchewan, nothing was done about it. That announcement was made, as I said, at a political convention of the provincial Tory party; the program which we were denied in parliament was announced at a Tory political convention with this fine disregard for the rights of parliament which unfortunately has been increasingly conspicuous in recent times. The government had promised to consider the suggestion which we put forward at that time and which was supported by all the members from Newfoundland. They promised to consider it when this question arose in the month of January; the Prime Minister told us on the second day of the session, I believe it was, that it was still under consideration. Two days later, or it may have been slightly longer, the Minister of Labour told us that the matter was not being considered.
At one stage of an earlier debate the minister said it was not considered because the proposal was made too late. That was the excuse he made. I point out that the suggestion was made earlier than the winter works program proposed to the municipalities, and that it would not have involved anybody except the federal government. There would have been no problem whatever about carrying it out had there been the will.
The alternative which the government followed-the alternative of making a start upon the building of community stages for fishing settlements-was a very good one, and I commend the government for undertaking it. It was very good for those settlements in which it was done. However, as my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo pointed out, of some 1,300 settlements around the coast of Newfoundland, 20 were affected by this plan to build community stages, and many of the individual projects could not be proceeded 
with last winter because the program was announced so late. Nevertheless, I may say that the people in those communities are grateful for what is being done.
I hope that next winter the scheme will be extended, and I hope the extension will be announced while we are still here. There is no reason why it should not be announced tomorrow. I can give the Minister of Fisheries a list of the settlements where these community stages would be of permanent benefit to the communities. I can provide him with that list any day he asks for it. The timber could be cut in the fall, and though construction cannot go on while there is ice in the sea, the work could be done early in the spring before the fishing season opens. That would be a real help. I know the Minister of Labour, who is genuinely interested in helping to alleviate unemployment, will at least give serious consideration to this suggestion.
With regard to the winter program itself, as the minister knows there are practically no municipalities in Newfoundland, apart from St. John's and Corner Brook, in the sense in which municipalities exist in other parts of the country, and this program in its original form, was not geared to conditions in Newfoundland at all, though this was the province with the greatest proportion of unemployment. It is true that a provision was subsequently made, as the minister pointed out one day in the house, and I want to be completely fair about this matter, enabling the province to act in lieu of a municipality.
Again, I do not intend to weary the committee by going back to the record, but if hon. members care to look at the speeches which were made by the Liberal members for Newfoundland on the last day of the session, or the day before the last day, and one day before that, they will see that we appealed to the government to implement term 29 of the terms of union without delay. I can tell the minister that if this had been done, and if that money had been paid at the time it should have been paid, and at the time the people of Newfoundland had a right to it, the treasury of Newfoundland would have been in a position to have done things under this winter works program which it has not been able to do. The denial by this government of money which rightfully belonged to the province under the constitution has already, I suspect, cost the province at least half a million dollars in unnecessary interest charges. That $500,000, if it had been spent on a winter work program, would have meant that instead of there being only 26 projects on which $49,000 was spent a very considerably greater sum might have been undertaken.

I myself know of many projects which were suggested but which the provincial government felt could not be proceeded with because there was just not enough leeway in the treasury. Why was this? It was because this government was not sufficiently interested to do something which would have caused very little debate in this house at that time. It was because the government failed to act upon a unanimous request of the house of assembly in Newfoundland asking that they should receive money to which they were entitled under the confederation agreement.
As the text said, to him that hath shall be given. And now we have insult added to injury, and a member of the present government goes to Newfoundland and claims, first of all, that the treasury has received money which has certainly not been paid. Even worse, he claims that the treasury has received funds whose payment has not yet even been authorized by parliament. The Minister of Justice told us this morning that $55 million had been paid into the treasury of Newfoundland last year. He told the board of trade last night that it was $100 million; then he found his arithmetic was all wrong, and changed it to $55 million. His arithmetic is still wrong, because as nearly as one can judge from the budget papers which I have in front of me the figures in respect of payments to Newfoundland including transitional and additional grants amount to $14.7 million. Of that $14.7 million, $13.5 million is called a special grant under the terms of union. Not only has that grant not been paid, but it has not even been voted.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: What has that got to do with the winter works program?

One of the reasons why the winter works program was almost a complete failure in Newfoundland was the neglect by this government of its duty to treat Newfoundland as the province has the right to be treated under the constitution, and if that is not related a great deal more to the minister's estimates than the debates about provincial matters we heard at earlier stages in this committee, I cannot think what would be.
Having made that point, I do not intend to continue on the subject because there will be another occasion on which to do so. I hope that occasion will not be long delayed, because this money has still not been voted. Until it is, and until it is made available, necessary services which would provide employment cannot be proceeded with.
I return to this 50-50 formula. The 50-50 formula makes it very easy for relatively
Supply-Labour
prosperous municipalities where the tax base is high and where unemployment is relatively low to embark on schemes for providing employment. But these projects do cause an additional strain upon areas which need help most, the areas where unemployment is highest. I say that this 50-50 method of dealing with this matter is utterly inadequate. It is not only inadequate in relation to the total number of unemployed in the country, but it is inadequate by reason of its method of application. I agree with the minister that we cannot expect this winter works program to provide for all the unemployed in this country. Nobody would be so foolish, I hope, as to suggest that. But to the extent that some employment can be provided in the winter time under this plan, the idea is a good one.
I believe that if an equitable provision is to be made for all Canadians, and if all are to be treated alike, a formula different from the 50-50 formula has to be provided. Indeed, it seems to me that particularly in the Atlantic provinces where unemployment has been regrettably at a much higher level than it has in any other part of the country and where there are in addition a good many very urgently needed federal works that, in some cases, could be timed a bit better-and I shall have something more to say about that when we are discussing the estimates of the Minister of Public Works, statements that have been made before in these debates- a greater effort should be made by the government to accelerate these works. The government should go on to provide a larger share of winter works directly in the form of federal works than has been done up to now.
I believe it was the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who said he felt sorry for the minister because his colleagues in the cabinet who are responsible for economic policy were not here during the consideration of the minister's estimates. These hon. gentlemen have a much larger share of the responsibility for the level of employment and the consequent level of unemployment than has the minister. I quite agree with what was said in this respect. I agree that it is the policies above of all of the Minister of Finance and to some degree of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and certain other ministers that have a much larger effect on determining the level of employment. The Minister of Labour because he happens to have the responsibility of the unemployment insurance commission must bear the brunt of criticisms that most of us direct not against the Minister of Labour but against the government as a whole with respect to the question of unemployment.
In spite of the recovery that is very marked and, which we on this side hope is going to

Supply-Labour
be very much more marked as the year goes on, we are going to have from this recent recession, as we have had from every recession since the war, an increasing number of people who are left stranded by the recession and the technological changes that follow a recession. In my opinion, one of the most useful suggestions made in this parliament for some time was the suggestion made a week ago by the hon. member for Trinity that a massive retraining program should be undertaken and this problem should not just be tossed off on the provincial governments or local authorities.
This is something for which a good foundation has been laid over the years by vocational grants, the progressive improvement of vocational schools and the progressive training of competent instructors in these schools. While everything cannot be done at once it is perfectly obvious that a very great deal more could be done. If we are going to meet the problems of change, instead of trying to bolster up uneconomic industries in the places where they are, a great deal along this line is going to have to be done and in a big way.
There is another problem that is relatively new. I am not criticizing the minister for this because it is not his responsibility at the present time. I am suggesting in some way or other it ought to be a responsibility of the unemployment insurance commission to see that the names of those who are unemployed for lengthy periods are kept in mind for employment opportunities as they arise.
We have the regrettable situation now that once a man or a woman has exhausted his stamps and ceases to get unemployment insurance there is a progressive tendency for that person to be forgotten and I am not blaming the commission for this because it is just in the nature of things. Such persons then have to go on provincial or local relief and while, if they are insistent enough, their names are kept on the rolls of the employment service, after a time they may be forgotten. I know there are many instances where this has happened and I know of experiences of this kind in the case of my own constituents whose names are dropped as dormant because these people having no income to live on except relief do not like to spend what little they have on 5 cent stamps to keep writing in to tell the offices to keep their names on the rolls. The result is that the people who have been out of work longest and need employment most and who should get first consideration receive last consideration. This was pointed out by several other hon. members and it is a particularly serious problem in Newfoundland with the
[Mr. Pickersglll.l
difficulties of communication we have there. In some way or other a radical new departure has to be made in this field.
I think the minister's department should give serious consideration to establishing some machinery for making sure that they keep track of those people and that an effort is made to see that they get a fair share of the employment that turns up. When a job comes along I do not blame the officials for saying, "Here is someone in St. John's who can do it," and forgetting that there are people in Bonavista who are equally competent to handle it. I do not blame them at all. However, we in parliament and especially those in the government should see that there is established machinery to prevent that happening. That is the point I am seeking to make and it is a highly important one.
Just as the St. Laurent government during the little recession of 1954-55 provided unemployment assistance on a 50-50 basis with the provinces, so a new step forward is going to have to be taken if we are going to have any considerable amount of continuing unemployment. I do not think a 50-50 contribution to relief is going to be adequate if the numbers are going to continue on unemployment relief that in some provinces were on unemployment relief in the past winter. I think we will have to go back and take another look at these proposals made by the government of which the hon. member for Essex East was a member in 1945. Those proposals were not put into effect, as everyone knows, because in the first place some of the provinces would not agree on them and in the second place because over a long period we had enjoyed virtually full employment or even more than full employment and the unemployment assistance problem was of a minor character, even in the winter time, until about 1954-55.
If this problem is going to drag on, even with a considerable measure of recovery, steps will have to be taken to solve it. In part because of the nature of the thing and in part because of the fact that an increasing number of people who are now unemployed are older people who experience difficulty in obtaining employment, a number are unskilled people and a number are people whose mobility is very limited; in view of all these circumstances the whole problem has to be looked at anew and in a different way.
A serious problem exists in Newfoundland despite what the Prime Minister said just a little over a year ago at Brantford. I just happen to have that reference before me and I have lots more like it. This appears in quotation marks and was reported in the Toronto Star of February 18, 1958, and is

an extract from a speech made the day before by the Prime Minister:
"The humblest of our people will not be forgotten," he promised. "The people who are unemployed will not be put in the false position of being put on relief."
There were no if's, and's or but's attached to that statement. It was unequivocal:
The people who are unemployed will not be put in the false position of being put on relief.
That was the promise upon which a good many of the 207 followers of the Prime Minister were elected to this house. That was the promissory note given on their behalf.
What do we find in the province of Newfoundland? In the month of March this year 7,018 families involving 37,321 persons received assistance in kind. Of these, 6,078 heads of families are employable. They and their dependants total 34,359 persons. I admit at once that, because of unemployment insurance for fishermen, that does include a considerable number of fishermen who were not able to qualify last year for unemployment insurance because of the failure of the fishery and that it was abnormally inflated on that account. But regardless of whether or not that is taken into account, it is a very different picture from this promise. It so happens that that is the state of affairs in a province with, unhappily, the lowest per capita income in the country, a province which by this government was denied its just due, denied the means that it was entitled to to help cope with this problem, a province which was left with this problem despite that promise of the Prime Minister.
I do think the people of Canada are going to hold the Prime Minister to account for that promise on every occasion on which they have the opportunity to hold him to account, and I think he should be held to account because the people should not be encouraged with that kind of promise if there is no intention whatever to implement it. It is simply playing ducks and drakes with human lives.
In view of the financial position of the country after two years of Tory government I do not expect that we are going to have the government assuming the whole responsibility for unemployment assistance but I do think that in some fashion or other the government has got to find a way to implement that pledge at least in spirit if they cannot do it in letter, and I do not believe, of course, that they ever will do it in letter. I am not going to say that I do not believe they ever intended to but I say I do not believe they will in fact do it in letter.
Supply-Labour
Oh, they likely will.

You mean after the unemployed are all dead. Perhaps the hon. member might listen to this quotation from the Prime Minister. I had not intended to read it again. It has been read into the record a good many times but it bears repetition. It is from his Charlottetown speech and the report appeared in the Toronto Star of February 28, 1958, a promise in quotation marks which has never been denied.
It would be the authority.

Well, it has been read over and over again and it has never been denied by the Prime Minister although he has had plenty of opportunities to deny it. The Prime Minister is pretty good at denying things. He denied the 15 per cent diversion of trade but he has never denied this. The report reads:
"I will make one more promise," the Prime Minister asserted.
"I have had experience, I know the lot of the average Canadian, I've gone through it," he said, dropping his voice and speaking in solemn tones.
Is that in there?
Yes, that is right, "dropping his voice and speaking in solemn tones."
He did not say that.
No, but this is a report by a very competent and reliable newspaperman.
There are reliable newspapers in Fredericton, too, Jack.
I know there are a lot of members, especially from Cape Breton island, who do not like to be reminded about this pledge of the Prime Minister.

The hon. member for
Bonavista-Twillingate does not want to be reminded of the affair in Fredericton either.
I will deal with the hon. gentleman and his affair in Fredericton any time it is relevant to the rules and I will just tell the hon. gentleman right now-
Order.

Oh, this is relevant. I am not going to deal with anything that is irrelevant. What did his leader and the maritime candidates promise at that great Atlantic assembly in Moncton in 1957? What did they promise? They promised that coal production would be increased in the maritime provinces and more employment would be given.

No, they did not; that is not so.

Supply-Labour
What has happened? They are now paying the fares of miners to go to northern Ontario. That is what is happening.
Talk about Manitoba.

Oh, I do not mind talking about Manitoba either. I will say this about Manitoba. Manitoba has suffered less from the recession than any other part of Canada because for years and years it had a good Liberal government running its affairs, a prudent government, and the lowest provincial taxation level in the country.
Why did they vote Tory then?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, I am going to come back-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must remind hon. members that one speaker has the floor at the present time and I would ask them to kindly refrain from interrupting too frequently. May I also remind the hon. member that we are discussing labour estimates and will he please relate his comments to the same.

I will be delighted to come back to this "let no one suffer" pledge. If hon. members have forgotten the beginning of it I can read it again but perhaps that would be trespassing unduly on the patience of the Minister of Labour. I continue with the quotation:
"I am not here for the purpose of telling of my experience in my early days until well into my late teens"-
What has that got to do with labour?

If the hon. gentleman would like to listen he would learn that this is in 1958 when the Prime Minister was really concerned about the plight of the unemployed. I continue:
"I know, I know ... a man who is unemployed is a human being, not a statistic.
That knowledge is not peculiar or special to the Prime Minister. The rest of us know it too.
"I make this promise. We acted."
I do not know in what sense he used the word "acted" but I leave it to hon. members to imagine. Certainly it was not in the sense of doing anything about the matter. The way they acted was to send parliament packing before we could see what a financial mess there was in the country brought about by their policies. They acted to have an election in order to make promises like this that have not been kept. That is the way they acted.
"We acted. My pledge is to every man and woman in this nation who is unemployed"-
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
To every man and woman in this nation who is unemployed.
-"so long as I am Prime Minister no one will be allowed to suffer in this nation."
There is lots more like this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, after all those long speeches by hon. members in the opposition, there is, of course, not much more to say. I thought that, somehow, there would be an end to the spate of words we have been hearing the last few days, first on the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and now on the estimates of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr).
Mr. Chairman, I have little to add. I just want to make a few remarks of general interest, and more particularly with regard to the people in my riding.

Without going into great detail I have outlined some of the work carried on in our department and through our advisory committees more will be carried on. This matter is of great importance to us and I wish to assure hon. members of this committee that no stone will be left unturned in the course of bringing about the most desirable results.

Mr. Chairman, the minister was good enough to answer the first part of my question but he did not answer the second part. Can the minister say if the rates he recommended to the treasury were based on the rates in Newfoundland or in the Maritime provinces?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether they were based on the maritimes or

Supply-Labour
Newfoundland rates. I do not have that information but I shall be glad to obtain it and give it to the hon. member at another time.

Mr. Chairman, under the proper item I should like to make some comments and ask some questions about the statistical press releases that are issued from time to time concerning the unemployed. The one in my hand is headed, "Unemployment Situation" and apparently was issued jointly by the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour.
That release is a joint release but the field work is done by the bureau of statistics and comes properly under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I am interested in the section concerning registrations at the national employment services. Is that a concern of the Department of Trade and Commerce?
No, Mr. Chairman, that comes under the national unemployment insurance commission and I shall be glad to deal with it under the appropriate item.

I will leave it until then. In the latter part of my remarks I made mention of uniformity of legislation as between the various acts under the minister's jurisdiction and similar types of legislation under provincial authorities. I wonder if any consultations have been held and if any steps have been taken toward meeting the question of uniformity of labour codes and labour legislation especially as they apply to corporations that have plants that are organized and consequently the same union is involved in more than one province. What have you been doing in that direction?

Mr. Chairman, I have given this matter quite a bit of thought. I am informed that in the past consultations did take place between the departments of labour of the federal and provincial governments. It is difficult to evolve a plan although I have been thinking about it and that is the stage at which it is now. I hope to be able to evolve a plan whereby it may be possible to achieve some uniformity with respect to vacations with pay and other labour legislation which is, I assume, what the hon. member has in mind.
When the minister says he is getting around to thinking about these matters I feel he should be reminded of the election promises made in this regard in the last two election campaigns.
Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact I keep a list on my desk and I am continually crossing out these promises as they are fulfilled.

Apparently the party did not keep you informed, Mr. Minister, of what they were letting you in for when they conducted the election campaigns because this was one of the promises made by the national Tory party and you as a candidate should have been advised as to what was happening. Perhaps they did not have you in mind as Minister of Labour at the time they developed this program. I wish to mention two points and while the opportunity presents itself I might as well mention some others. One promise made was that there would be co-operation with the provinces in an effort to achieve uniformity of labour legislation. That cannot be done just by thinking about it and there must be action.
It takes time, too.

Yes, I realize that, but this was two years ago in 1957. Two years have elapsed since then. I appreciate that the minister has been extremely busy.
Another thing the national Tory party failed to tell the minister about was the question of industries that cut across provincial boundaries. They were to pay special attention to the meat packing and steel industries to promote uniformity of labour legislation. I wonder if the party advised the minister prior to his appointment that they also promised to extend the provisions of the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act to cover all federal government contracts and projects? I wonder if this has been done and if they have been able to accomplish their promise of eliminating delays in conciliation procedures? I also wonder what steps have been taken toward introducing new amendments to the Minimum Wages Act? The question of vacations with pay has been dealt with. While we are at it, I wonder if in fulfillment of the promises the Tories made they have been able to move toward eliminating the waiting period under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act and extending coverage to the greatest possible number of wage earners or whether they are still just thinking about that one?
I bring these points to the attention of the minister because it is obvious he was not kept up to date concerning what the national Tory party was getting him into when conducting the election campaign of 1957.

Mr. Chairman, before the item is carried I want to renew my appeal to the government-I see that the leader of the house is here now-to do what was invariably done by all other governments, to accede to the reasonable request of the opposition to let this item stand until the end of the session or until the government is in a
