subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Pori Arthur) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-14, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952, with respect to the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last year when this bill was introduced I was fortunate enough that it was discussed for several hours and a relatively worthwhile debate took place in connection with its merits. I am not one of those who feel that a politician is suspect whenever he gets up and begins to talk about

the beauties of non-partisanship just as I do not suspect, when people begin to talk about the public interest, that there is possibly a scoundrel or a nigger in the woodpile somewhere. I should like to suggest that if one cannot be wholly non-partisan about this bill he should at least try to approach it with as little partisanship as possible.
The reason I have introduced it stems partly from my own experience and partly from following the activities of the house in this particular field over recent years and also in a historical sense. I made the point last year, and I do not need to repeat it, that the idea behind redistribution being put in the hands of an independent commission is one that has found favour with such people as the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the prime minister who was the leader of Canada for the longest period of time, an hon. gentleman in the other place who is a Liberal stalwart and with quite a number of other people, and that the idea of putting redistribution under an independent commission is one that has found favour in a number of other commonwealth countries that have the same parliamentary system as we have, although not necessarily with parallel problems, where it has been found to work well.
The basic idea of redistribution is, of course, simply one of representation by population or an attempt to assure that each individual vote in the country is worth relatively the same as any other individual vote. I would not say that the material I put on the record last session was so valuable that I want to hold it up as being something wonderful but I think the bibliography and other information connected with it opened up many of the problems concerning the matter and some of the discussion that followed was rather valuable in expressing critical points of view.
One factor in connection with redistribution about which I have thought more and more since last year is not the fact that we are getting closer to the issue all the time of a hurried redistribution in 1952 or that we will probably find an election held in 1962 upon the population basis of 1951 but the fact that it seems to me after a bit more experience in the house, and everyone is aware that my experience has not been too long, that a member more and more, if I judge the situation correctly, is becoming a constituency information and welfare officer to quite an extent for the population of his riding. I mean that the pressure upon him is in direct relationship to the size of his constituency. This is an argument which, in my opinion, calls for as fair a balance as

possible within provincial limitations, and for equality in terms of the number of people that a member of parliament represents.
During the debate on this measure last year, the lead-off speaker following my presentation was the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), who opposed the bill largely on the ground, as I take it from scanning his remarks, that the bill was a further derogation of parliamentary rights. He believed that in setting up an independent commission you were taking away from parliament and this house certain rights, and that was something he could not support. In so far as my argument was concerned that by so doing you would remove any chance for gerrymandering, both he and the hon. member who spoke later, the hon. member for St. Lawrence - St. George (Mr. Chambers), had the feeling that we had reached a new time in Canadian politics. Perhaps their views are coloured by the fact that they are members of the party in power. They felt we no longer have any worries about anyone trying to hurt anyone else. We have a population that is more alert, more informed, and this sort of thing would not be accepted any longer.
I cannot really comment on that particular point of view. It is going to be fun, during the next redistribution, to see what the members from Nova Scotia are going to do, since they are all Conservatives, in reducing the seats in that province. There will be a reduction of at least one, and it is going to be fun to see how much they hurt one another. In Saskatchewan, where there will be a loss of three or four seats, the Conservatives have only the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) upon whom to work in terms of gerrymandering. Then, too, I should like to see them work on each other in Manitoba, where they can only work on themselves. We could almost turn the problem inside out from the point of view of gerrymandering being an issue, and say that at least an independent commission would save government members from cutting each other's throats when redistribution time does come around.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) spoke on the bill, but I felt it was one of his poorer performances. He was thrown off by some of the comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), and by our wonder interventionist from Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). The hon. member proceeded to read the members of this group a little homily about our too great preoccupation with planning and our too great trust in experts. He did, however, state he thought there
British North America Act should be some kind of independent body of experts or knowledgeable people to determine principles which should apply in so far as redistribution was concerned, then those principles should be left with members of parliament who would deal with redistribution. He seemed to feel that members of parliament, being more familiar with constituency problems, were the ones to be consulted. I should like to remind the hon. member for York-Scarborough or any other member, including myself, that much as we may look upon our constituencies as our personal possessions, our rights are very impermanent ones. There are other parties within our constituencies who have views that are just as valid and as pertinent as any we, as members of parliament, can offer. We are only one source of information or opinion, and there are other sources of information and opinion which are just as important in so far as determining the boundaries of a constituency and that sort of thing is concerned.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is he suggesting-he seemed to me to be suggesting and perhaps he can tell me if I am right-that perhaps the defeated candidate should be consulted in determining the riding boundaries?

No, I am not trying to suggest that at all. I do not believe the defeated candidate or someone who ran third, fourth or fifth or who is the head of a local organization, is in any better position than an M.P. to be consulted. My whole point is that they have as valid an interest as the member of parliament. I would say that any independent commission gathering information would want to hear representations from these people on this question of boundaries.
I seem to have forgotten the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who, along with the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), concentrated on an argument which is very familiar to anyone who has watched the Quebec scene. In my opinion, the source of their argument can be found in the Tremblay report, in which the line of argument is strongly adopted that redistribution concerns one part of the British North America Act that requires provincial consultation. As a matter of fact, I think the hon. member for Joliette - L'Assomption - Montcalm adopted exactly the idea that is in the Tremblay report, that once the bases have been determined for general provincial representation,

British North America Act the whole problem should be handled by the province itself rather than the House of Commons. In my view this is an indefensible position, in that the House of Commons must continue to hold the right to set up, for example, this independent commission, and if the independent commission does not work, to make any other amendment or change that is necessary.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere was generally in favour of the idea of putting redistribution under a commission, but he did want this exception, that the commission should be determined on a provincial basis and the provincial authorities should enter into it. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George brought up a legal point as to whether or not the words "independent commission" were really valid because of the fact that parliament would always have the right to change a decision made some years ago about this section, and to change it or alter it at any time. In other words, you may set up an independent commission but it would not be there in perpetuity, so therefore it would not be an independent commission.
This is rather a difficulty in semantics. 1 agree with his point that if we do set up an independent commission as a consequence of the passage of this particular act, then we will have to remain ready to change the independent commission idea if it does not work out. I might point out in passing that the independent commission idea, for example, in Great Britain has worked extremely well. The same fears were expressed in Great Britain as were expressed by hon. members on the government benches here when this change was sought.
There were no speeches made by hon. members of the opposition when this bill was before us last year. This has become one of the hallmarks of their operations in this particular parliament, that is they do not express any opinion on public bills introduced by private members. I just want to touch on this particular aspect of the matter. The opposition members may not see the point or feel the need of this particular hour of the house activities, they may not feel that this idea of private members being able to introduce public bills is worth while. However, it seems to me that at some time we should have a statement from this particular party, not so much about this bill, but on this issue of whether or not they believe this sort of thing is even worth while. In my opinion, it is very worth while because it leaves to hon. members at least one avenue by which private members from any party can put a bill on the order paper expounding an idea

or conception, and ultimately the idea may become popular. If the members of the opposition feel that this is a bad thing, and that all legislation should come up through some sort of party channel in the government, then they are accepting the fact we have already had a transition in the status of a member of parliament and that the rest of us may be clinging to some ideal that has disappeared.
The final point I want to make is not a major one. It is just this, that the Canadian Labour Congress has advocated this idea of redistribution by an independent commission for some time. I could go further than that. I could also say that another body has identified itself with this idea of an independent commission. I refer to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I would suggest-and perhaps not push the suggestion too far-that when you get two bodies such as these that in the main contend with each other or are antithetical both going along with the same idea, the idea must have a little bit more than ordinary value.
I hope in the time there is left some of the members will be able to express further criticisms and offer further suggestions on the bill. I would hope that some of them might even move that this bill be sent to the committee on privileges and elections which I am sure is going to do an extremely worth-while job this session. I might say this about the chairman of that committee at the present time. Nothing has pleased me more than to know that in this particular field we have as chairman of that committee someone who has an academic background and with the broad values and detachment that I think that background brings to one of the most controversial fields that politicians can ever get into.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are all grateful to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) for his summary of the arguments we dared to advance in the face of his final utterances on the subject. It seems to me to be rather typical of the hon. member sponsoring this measure and other members in his group. I have stated this previously in this house and shall state it again. There seems to be a theory that, once these omnipotent people have examined a subject and written down their conclusions, that is the end of it; that everything that needs to be thought about this subject has been thought and that everything that needs to be said about the subject has been said. The leader of the lonely eight earlier in this session went farther than that and suggested that owing to the fact that he had introduced a certain measure

into this house on three or four occasions there was no need for any further debate whatsoever.
However, to come back to the bill in question, may I say this. I would be derelict indeed in my duty as a member of this house if I did not rise on each and every appropriate occasion in order to draw attention to the plight of the people of York-Scarborough. As I have said before in this house, the pattern of growth in this particular constituencey is astonishing, to say the least. The population at the present time would be something of the order of 225,000 people. As far as I can gather, the annual increase in that population-apart from the birth rate which is substantial-is something of the order of 25,000 a year. I have given serious consideration to introducing a private bill which might be entitled "An act for the relief of McGee" or perhaps might be better described as "An act for the relief of the long-suffering and patient constituents of Y ork-Scarborough".
I should like to read into the record a statement by one of my opponents in the last election and the one prior to it, namely a charming and delightful woman indeed by the name of Elva Reta Sigen. Mrs. Sigen took advantage of the opportunity, she having been a candidate in federal elections, to write in August of 1957 to the chief electoral officer offering some suggestions. I will not deal with the specific suggestions and criticisms of the operation of the elections act because they are not pertinent to this debate-they might form part of the evidence of the committee in privileges and elections- but I should like to read into the record her first paragraph:
As a candidate in the federal election in June. I would like to take this opportunity accorded me tn section 58(2) of the Canada Elections Act to bring to your attention a few changes in the law which I consider desirable in so far as it affects the riding of York-Scarborough.
The first paragraph I refer to reads as follows:
(1) For an urban riding York-Scarborough is unwieldy, being the largest riding in Canada with a population at present of 167,500 people and with more families moving into the riding every day. If this growth continues, it will be an impossible task for any candidate to campaign and for any member to represent the riding and know the problems of such a large number of people.
As I say, these are the words of my opponent in the two previous elections. She is a woman of some ability and much charm. They were no doubt prompted by the fact that her father was a prominent Tory in the good old riding of Carleton.
As the hon. member pointed out, I agreed in principle with his bill but I expressed
British North America Act some doubts, after I survived the interruptions and banter that assailed me on that occasion. I thought at a certain stage the independent commission or group of so-called experts should come back to the house and to the members, having defined the broad areas and designated the principles upon which such distribution would occur. I am one of those optimists, like the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) and others in this house, who happens to believe that as far as political morality in this country is concerned, tremendous strides have been made in recent years. Everything that I see in the political life of my province and in my area in particular leads me to the belief that this trend and pattern will continue.
I was going to read into the record some of the delightful experiences and activities which took place in the early years in elections in this country but I am sure that most of the hon. members who have interested themselves in this bill and in this matter are already familiar with this subject. As Norman Ward says in his book, honesty is becoming compulsory in many parts of this country.
Would you like to define the parts?

The problem, and the reasons advanced in another debate earlier in this session by the hon. member for Port Arthur as to why we might not have redistribution before the next election, I challenge. As far as its being possible is concerned, surely the methods and means are now available today, particularly as far as tabulation and computation are concerned, if some way can be found between the spring of 1961 and the beginning of the session in 1962, assuming that an election is called at the end of that particular session. Surely the basic material can be made available to this house and to the members of whatever body we ultimately decide will wrestle with this problem, and surely we can have redistribution before the next election. I see the hon. member is shaking his head.

May I ask the hon. member a question. Is the hon. member aware that it is technically impossible before March, 1962 for the bureau of statistics to complete its compilations of the detailed statistics which will be necessary to carry out complete redistribution, even though the total population statistics by provinces will be available much earlier in order to give a provincial breakdown? But you will not have the detailed figures which will enable you to actually carry out adjustments.

British North America Act
May I, in turn, ask the hon. member a question. What is the source of the information or opinion which he has expressed?
The information I have is from the dominion bureau of statistics officials.
Well, as one hon. member has just pointed out to me, a lot of things which perhaps were not thought possible under other administrations might very well be possible under the present.
Possible but improbable.

That is just about all I wanted to add, Mr. Speaker, to what I said last year, except I have to apologize to the hon. member for Port Arthur that I did not come up to snuff last year and I hope he will think I did a little better this year.

Mr. Speaker, it is largely the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat which cause me to rise to say a few words in support of this bill introduced by the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). This is not a new subject. Anyone who has read the records of the house will realize that there have been quite a few voices in all parties over a long period of years who have suggested some procedure for redistribution after the fashion of that mentioned in this bill. The member for Port Arthur referred to the attitude of the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, who I think on a number of occasions-if I remember correctly I heard him on one such occasion -said that while he personally was in favour of the principle of having redistribution undertaken by a commission, he would accept the opinion of the majority. There have occasionally been other voices raised in the Liberal party throughout the years, and I think on one or two occasions members of the former Progressive party suggested that this principle be applied with respect to redistribution in Canada.
It has been the policy of the C.C.F. party ever since it was formed to express its support for this method of redistribution, and that is indicated by the numbers of private bills which have been introduced on this question by members of the C.C.F. group throughout the years. However, I do want to bring to the attention of the house, in view of the comments made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, that at one time there were quite prominent members of the Progressive Conservative party who supported this principle. On February 21, 1947 the then secretary of state introduced a bill for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. That

provided for the appointment of a committee. During that debate Mr. Knowles, who was then a member of this house, introduced an amendment to the bill which read as follows, as reported on page 697 of Hansard for February 21, 1947:
-this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons should be referred to an independent commission to be appointed for that purpose.
Then later on certain members of the Progressive Conservative party spoke and indicated their support of that amendment. The interesting thing to me is that at the tune when the vote was taken on this amendment, who do we find supporting the amendment moved by Mr. Knowles which would provide for the appointment of a commission to undertake redistribution? Well, here are the names of some of them. We find Mr. Black, who was then a Conservative member for the Yukon; Mr. Blair, then a Conservative member of this house but who unfortunately passed away two or three years ago; Mr. Boucher, a Conservative member; Mr. Casselman; Mr. Cockeram; Mr. Fraser, who is still in this house; and Mr. Harkness, who is now the present Minister of Agriculture. Then, most interesting to me of all, is the name of Mr. Green, who is now the present Minister of Public Works and the house leader.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: How do you know I will not support this bill?

Then we find Mr. Harris, a Conservative member of this house; Mr. Hatfield; Mr. Henderson; Mr. Homuth. Then we come again to another interesting supporter, Mr. Macdonnell, the present Minister without Portfolio. Then we find Mr. Merritt, a well-known Conservative, still residing at the coast. Mr. Senn, a very prominent member of the Conservative party at that time; Mr. Stirling, who used to represent the riding of Yale. That is all I see in the list, but I think it is very interesting in view of the support that that proposal received from those very prominent members of the Progressive Conservative party, some of whom are now members of the government.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, that leads us in this group to the hope that possibly before the next redistribution we will see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) rising to introduce a bill for the appointment of a commission to undertake redistribution, seconded by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell).

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It does not come under public works.

I quite understand that. It comes under the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche); but I assume the Minister of Public Works might be so enthusiastic as to undertake that task, or at least speak of it.
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in reading Hansard to note that the idea was also born within the womb of the Liberal party, because on February 21, 1947, Mr. Powers, who was then a member of this house and who is now an hon. member of the other place, informed the house that in looking over his files he had found a copy of a bill which had been drafted, and it was the intention of the government at one time to introduce this bill which made provision for the appointment of a commission to undertake redistribution. However, owing to the fact that in 1940 the phony stage of the war, as he put it, was over and the nation was fully occupied with the realities of war, the bill was not introduced. So, Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that there has been considerable sentiment throughout the years in favour of a commission undertaking the task of redistribution.
That principle has been supported by prominent members of the Liberal party and it has been supported by prominent members of the Conservative party. It is a principle which has been consistently supported by all members of the C.C.F. group in this house throughout the years. As one of our members said previously this afternoon, we would not be at all offended if the present government, shall we say, stole this plank from our platform and gave effect to it before the next redistribution.
I do want to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time we gave some consideration to this principle. It has been adopted by several other countries in the commonwealth and found to be most satisfactory, and in handing the task over to a commission it would remove the injustices and the doubts with regard to redistribution which exist at the present time.
We do hope that hon. members on the front benches will be consistent and give expression to their attitude first expressed in February 1947 by introducing legislation from the government side giving effect to the principles contained in this private bill.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill, I wish only to add a few remarks to those made by members who spoke before me.
The amendment put forward by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) is most
British North America Act interesting. However, before allowing it to pass, I think we should at least have a closer look at it.
I have been going over the statistics quoted to us last year by the hon. member for Port Arthur, which gave specific information on the number of voters, the area and total population of every constituency in Canada. Such information is most interesting, and I often wonder how opposition members, and particularly C.C.F. members, manage to find time to make such elaborate research into various fields, and also to make lengthy speeches on practically every subject discussed in this house. In any case, this is not the question we are considering at present.
I would like to point out to this house that, in his remarks, the hon. member for Port Arthur admitted that the amendment he was moving under Bill C-14 would not reach its aim, which was to make redistribution independent by adding to the British North America Act the words "independent of the Canadian parliament". His suggestion to refer the redistribution of parliament seats to a body independent of the Canadian parliament is only theoretical, as parliament can, in fact, always amend the act. And in order to further clarify the reasons for which we should be very careful before passing such legislation, I would simply like to point out to hon. members what happens, for instance, when redistribution is made in vast territories in which population is perhaps not as dense as in our large Canadian cities like Montreal and Toronto, but which nevertheless are entitled to representation in this house, so as to make the Canadian government aware of the needs of people in those areas.
Let us take for instance the riding I represent here. The constituency of Chapleau was created in 1933 on the occasion of a redistribution and it covers 83,640 square miles. In 1937, it had 30,094 voters, out of a population of 65,456. The neighbouring riding, that of Villeneuve, covers 5,250 square miles. It had in 1957, 34,494 voters and a total population of 74,366. That riding was created in 1947. Further to the south, there is the constituency of Pontiac-Temiscamingue which has an area of 16,625 square miles with 20,480 voters and a total population of 42,432. Those three constituencies therefore cover 105,515 square miles, and include 85,068 electors out of a total population of 182,244, according to the latest available statistics. I should like to point out that before 1933, that area contained only one constituency, before the constituency of Chapleau was itself carved out and that, in

British North America Act 1947, part of the constituency of Pontiac-Temiscamingue was cut out, in order to give the mining area of Rouyn, Noranda, Malar-tic and Val d'Or, a representation in the house.
In establishing the constituency of Ville-neuve and in adopting the amendments which were proposed to readjust those territories, account was taken not only of the population but also of that northern territory which is developing rapidly, since, even if sometimes the population is not as large as in cities those territories are, just the same, entitled to representation in the Canadian parliament.
That leads me to say, in closing, that since confederation, and generally speaking, changes were made to several constituencies. Making a brief survey of the situation, I noted that in the maritimes, for instance, there were changes made in 22 constituencies. In the province of Ontario, there were changes made in 76 constituencies; in the province of Quebec, 60; in the western provinces, 46 constituencies and in British Columbia, 22 constituencies. Between 1892 and 1952 changes were made in 226 constituencies. Therefore, since confederation,
i.e. since 1867, only 37 constituencies have remained unchanged. In other words, readjustment of several constituencies is taking place regularly according to changes in population, from one end of our huge country to the other.
So, instead of agreeing to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur, and as was suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), it would be preferable, in my opinion, to set up a commission which would be responsible for the readjustment of electoral seats in the federal parliament.

I am happy to have the opportunity to participate briefly, as needs must at this hour, in this debate. I should like to say how much I appreciate the kind remarks of the hon. gentleman from Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who is, I suppose, spatially as far removed from me as anyone could be in this chamber, and to congratulate him for his efforts in this direction.
I remember quite well his contributions, both written and oral, during the last session. The hon. member also brought us up to date with an appraisal of the speeches which were delivered. He did not appraise his own, and

I noted his modesty in that connection, but he did comment on the others. He is quite right in saying there is today an overwhelming tendency to approach this important subject with a high degree of impartiality. It is, indeed, a subject which is of tremendous importance. And as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) pointed out, it is, of course, not a new subject.
For members of parliament to direct their attention to means and methods whereby they may improve their ability to express fully and honestly the opinions of the general public is certainly a very high form of endeavour, for we are here to express public opinion-in an indirect democracy this makes us the most important expressive institution in the land.
I have long been interested in the subject of independent commissions for distribution of electoral constituencies. I have had many reasons to see in them very favourable aspects. I believe that the province of Manitoba recently moved into the field with an independent commission and in recent hours I have come to the conclusion that this sort of device is not too bad and does allow for a very good expression of popular opinion on election day.
Some hon. members on this side of the house have expressed themselves quite well when they pointed out that the mores of the country have changed. I believe that the evil old days of the past cannot return. Certainly there are many historical instances which should bring to us a blush of shame. It is known that many an infamous old gerrymander occurred in the days of Conservative administration and instances of this have unhappily occurred in much more recent days. I am sure that if the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) were here he would tell us of some personal experiences. We might remember what happened in Parry Sound-Muskoka at one time. We could recall the marriage of the Brandon and Souris ridings and the death of the Lake Centre riding all taking place at one time. These were very unhappy examples of parliamentary activity in this connection.
Through the years I think it has been shown that gerrymanders are not a sure-fire recipe for success. Perhaps the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) was not altogether humorous when he said that honesty in this instance is proving to be the better policy. In the voting pattern of citizens I believe there are reasons for this.

Once upon a time we looked upon certain areas or constituencies in a province as being hidebound and devotedly attached to a given party regardless of candidate, issue or any other consideration. It was felt there were certain blocs of safe seats and if one could only attach and detach them in some logical mathematical proportion one could win political success. But we have moved far away from the days of hereditary voting. If you could squelch a party by manoeuvring political boundaries of constituencies the party which is now in power in Canada would have been kept in the shadows for years and years if not forever. The party, however, revealed its ability to fight in any constituency in Canada and it won nearly all of them. I say this in no sense of gloating or boasting but as an indication of the fact that the pattern of voting has changed. I believe this is a very good development and I am sure the promoter of this bill would agree that the hereditary pattern of voting is not an uplifting aspect of a political democracy.
There are some underlying issues in this matter that might be worth exploring. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) said on a previous occasion to the effect that any move to shift power and responsibility from the elective and responsible institution of government to one which is not elective and is irresponsible in a constitutional sense is not a step which should be taken lightly. Down through the years in the British tradition a great effort was made to bring under popular control the agencies of government, to bring the executive under parliamentary control and to move away from the earlier day when the rule of law did not prevail over these agencies and aspects of state sovereignty. In this instance I am not prepared to move to this too readily or gladly. I believe that the intervention of parliamentary responsibility is a very good thing.
In this connection I remember last year that the hon. member was good enough to put forward a very extensive and interesting bibliography and I was happy to see included in it the works of many of my former colleagues in the field of political science. I would not presume to tell anyone what he should read but had I more time at my disposal I had intended to make reference to a very important work which I am sure is familiar to many hon. members of the house, "The New Despotism" by the Right Hon. Lord Hewart of Bury, in which he deals with this growing tendency in these days of big government and of demands for
Business of the House
government to move into more and more avenues of daily life, with the dangers inherent in setting up regulatory bodies which are not directly responsible to the organ which in turn is responsible to the sovereign people.
Another aspect we must consider is that the mere counting of heads is not of itself a sufficient consideration. We in Canada are a pragmatic and practical people and we do not follow neat formulae. If we were to follow a certain precise formula under which a certain number of people had one member of parliament and this prevailed all across the country, it would be unworkable. I know that the hon. member does not have this in mind because I remember the thesis he put forward. There are also historic and geographic considerations which must be involved and I do not think that because one citizen lives in a constituency which has 50,000 voters and another lives in a constituency which has 25,000 voters the quality of the representation of the former in this sovereign parliament is any less and certainly no one would say it is only half as good.
This is not to say, however, that such complaints as the hon. member for York-Scarborough put forward with deep feeling are not to be considered seriously and do not cry for early remedy. At the same time I do not think there is any mystical efficacy in the mathematical computation of voters and the election thereby-
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does the hon. member think there is any mystical efficacy in the practice that protects Prince Edward Island and keeps it with four members?

Mr. Speaker, I wish I had more time to talk about Prince Edward Island's membership. I think that is just one instance of what we have been talking about. Indeed, had our negotiators in 1873 insisted on a minimum of six seats I think they would have served not only Prince Edward Island but Canada better than they did. Six seats were accepted but this number was eventually and over many protests reduced to four.
